adversarial.note: every word is a rotation of the same 10-letter multiset, so all n words share one anagram signature (one exact dict key, not merely one hash bucket) and land in a single group; empirically this does NOT degrade to O(n^2) the way distinct-but-colliding keys do, since CPython dicts resolve a repeated exact key by direct slot lookup rather than probing a chain — see README

complexity.notes: Each word's key is computed twice (once in the dict comprehension and again in the append loop); a single pass with collections.defaultdict(list) would be cleaner and avoid duplicate work. The return annotation 'tuple(int)' is not a valid type hint — use tuple[int, ...] from Python 3.9+. The keys are a bounded fixed-size signature, so lookups remain O(1) even in the worst case.
complexity.summary: Computes a 26-element character-count tuple as a canonical key for each word, groups words by that key in a dict, then returns the grouped values.

complexity.notes: The best_buy variable (and its initialization to 100) is computed but never used — dead code left over from an intended single-pass O(n) approach. The solution is correct but could be reduced to one pass by tracking the minimum price seen so far and maximizing prices[i] - best_buy. Consider range(len(prices)) vs. range(len(prices)-1) — the -1 is fine but the unused best_buy update should be removed.
complexity.summary: Brute force: for each index i as a buy day, iterates over all later indices j as sell days, tracking the maximum profit seen.

complexity.notes: Initializing best_buy to 100 relies on the stated constraint prices[i] <= 100, which is guaranteed, but float('inf') would be more idiomatic and constraint-independent. Iterating with 'for price in prices' would also be cleaner than indexing.
complexity.summary: Single pass tracking the minimum price seen so far (best_buy) and the maximum profit of selling at each day, returning the best profit found. Since best_profit starts at 0, the no-transaction case is handled automatically.

complexity.notes: The debug print inside the loop should be removed (it also adds O(n) I/O overhead), and the math.ceil expressions in it are both unused for the logic and mathematically incorrect for the fleet check (integer ceilings can wrongly equate distinct arrival times) — only the float division comparison is correct. Using sorted(zip(position, speed)) would be more idiomatic than the index-based list comprehension. Starting result at 1 is safe only because the constraints guarantee n >= 1.
complexity.summary: Pairs each car's position and speed, sorts by position, then scans from the car nearest the target backward: a trailing car merges into the lead fleet if its arrival time is no greater than the lead's, otherwise it starts a new fleet and becomes the new lead. Sorting dominates the runtime; the scan is linear.

complexity.notes: Storing tuples (temp, index) works, but storing only indices and comparing temperatures[stack[-1]] would be slightly cleaner and avoid redundant data.
complexity.summary: Uses a monotonic decreasing stack of (temperature, index) pairs; when a warmer temperature arrives, it pops all cooler pending days and records the day difference. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, giving linear time.

adversarial.note: n distinct multiples of 2**61-1, all hashing to 0, so every dict insert/lookup collides

complexity.notes: The variable name `dict` shadows the built-in; a set with early exit (return True on first repeat) or `len(set(nums)) != len(nums)` would be simpler and avoid the second pass.
complexity.summary: Counts occurrences of each value in a dictionary over one pass, then makes a second pass to check whether any value has a count greater than 1.

complexity.notes: int(a/b) converts through a float, which can lose precision or raise OverflowError for very large intermediate products (possible in theory given the constraints); a pure-integer truncating division such as (abs(a)//abs(b)) * (1 if (a<0)==(b<0) else -1) would be safer. Minor style point: chained if/elif on operator strings is fine, but a dict mapping operators to lambdas would be more idiomatic.
complexity.summary: Classic stack-based RPN evaluation: push operands, and on each operator pop two values, apply the operation, and push the result. Handles subtraction/division operand order explicitly and truncates division toward zero.

complexity.notes: The try/except around the comparison loops is unidiomatic and masks potential bugs; a plain length check plus one comparison loop (or simply multiset_s == multiset_t) would be cleaner. The redundant second loop is unnecessary since equal-sized multisets with matching counts for s's keys already match t's. Consider collections.Counter for the multiset logic.
complexity.summary: Builds character-frequency multisets for both strings via dicts, then compares the two multisets key-by-key (in both directions) to verify equality. Because keys are lowercase English letters, each dict holds at most 26 entries, so all lookups are O(1) even in the worst case.

complexity.notes: s.lower() creates an O(n) copy; comparing characters case-insensitively inline (e.g., via s[a].lower()) would give O(1) auxiliary space. The inner right-pointer loop could in theory be guarded against underflow for clarity, though it is safe here since the left pointer always rests on an alphanumeric character first.
complexity.summary: Two-pointer scan from both ends of the lowercased string, skipping non-alphanumeric characters and comparing the remaining characters pairwise.

complexity.notes: Clean and idiomatic; a two-pointer approach would reduce extra space to O(1) but the O(n) auxiliary string is acceptable given n <= 1000.
complexity.summary: Filters the lowercased string to alphanumeric characters, then checks whether the cleaned string equals its reverse.

complexity.notes: The expand-and-remove strategy is correct and each element is visited once, but the more idiomatic approach only expands from sequence starts (x where x-1 not in set), which avoids mutating the set and is arguably clearer. Set membership relies on average-case hashing; adversarial hash collisions could degrade lookups to O(n), yielding O(n^2) worst case.
complexity.summary: Builds a set of the numbers, then repeatedly pops an arbitrary element and expands outward in both directions, removing each visited element so every value is processed exactly once. Tracks the maximum run length found.

complexity.notes: Correctly handles duplicate minimums by pushing on <= and popping only on equality. Initializing min_stack with float('inf') avoids an empty-check in push; all operations are cleanly O(1) with no hashing involved.
complexity.summary: Maintains a main stack plus an auxiliary min stack that records each new running minimum (including duplicates), so getMin is just a peek at the min stack's top; pop discards the min entry only when the popped value equals the current minimum.

complexity.notes: Uses division (prod // num), which the follow-up explicitly asks to avoid — the standard prefix/suffix product approach would be preferable. Slicing nums[:zero] and nums[zero+1:] creates unnecessary O(n) copies, and the match statement with a guarded first case is more verbose than simple if/elif. Correctness is fine given the constraints.
complexity.summary: Handles zeros as special cases: if there are multiple zeros the answer is all zeros; with one zero, only the zero position gets the product of the rest; otherwise it computes the total product and divides by each element.

complexity.notes: Correct under the stated ASCII-only constraint, but the trick breaks for the follow-up (arbitrary Unicode input), where a length-prefixed encoding would be required. The decode of the empty list works incidentally: ''.split(delimiter) yields [''] and pop(-1) clears it, though this is subtle and worth a comment.
complexity.summary: Encodes by joining the strings with an emoji delimiter (plus a trailing delimiter) and decodes by splitting on that delimiter and dropping the final empty segment. Since the delimiter is a non-ASCII character and input strings are guaranteed to be ASCII-only, it can never collide with string content.

complexity.notes: Correctness is fragile: since strings may contain any ASCII characters, a string containing the literal delimiter would break decoding; a length-prefixed encoding (e.g., 'len#string') is the robust standard approach. Also decode('') incidentally returns [] only via the pop(-1) trick, which is non-obvious.
complexity.summary: Encodes by joining the strings with a fixed sentinel delimiter (plus a trailing sentinel), and decodes by splitting on that delimiter and dropping the empty trailing piece. Both join and split scan the total character volume once, which scales linearly with n.

complexity.notes: Decode would be O(n) if it tracked an integer offset into the original string instead of reassigning `s` to a sliced copy each iteration. `s.index('|')` also scans from position 0 each time, though with bounded per-string lengths this is secondary to the slicing cost.
complexity.summary: Encodes each string as `length|content` concatenated together; decode repeatedly finds the next `|`, parses the length prefix, extracts that many characters, and re-slices the remainder. Encoding is linear in total characters, but decoding is quadratic because each iteration copies the remaining string with `s = s[...:]`.

complexity.notes: Counting is non-idiomatic; num_counts[num] = num_counts.get(num, 0) + 1 or collections.Counter would be cleaner. The final loop re-scans all items for each of the k thresholds (O(k*d)), which is fine only because k <= 5 and d <= 2001; a single pass selecting keys by a threshold frequency would be simpler. Relying on the stated uniqueness guarantee for correctness of the tie handling is valid, but the list(set(output)) de-dup is a code smell suggesting the tie logic is fragile.
complexity.summary: Builds a frequency dict in one pass, sorts the distinct frequency values and keeps the top k, then collects every key whose count equals one of those top-k frequencies. The problem's uniqueness guarantee ensures the frequency scan yields exactly k elements, and the value bound (-1000..1000) caps distinct keys at 2001, making the sort and scans effectively constant.

complexity.notes: Correct but unidiomatic and fragile: the index()/pop() index-recovery logic is convoluted and each index() call is an O(n) scan. A one-pass hashmap (value -> index) achieves O(n) time far more cleanly, or sort (value, index) pairs to avoid the index-recovery hack entirely.
complexity.summary: Sorts a copy of the array and uses a two-pointer scan to find the pair summing to target, then recovers the original indices with nums.index(), with a pop-based workaround for duplicate values.

adversarial.note: n distinct multiples of 2**61-1 (already ascending), all hashing to 0, so every dict insert/lookup collides

complexity.notes: Sorting is unnecessary since the input is guaranteed sorted, and the nums2 copy makes the solution O(n) extra space, violating the problem's O(1) space requirement. The repeated O(n) index() calls and pop() add linear overhead and convoluted duplicate handling; a plain two-pointer on the original array with offset +1 indices would be simpler, O(n) time, and O(1) space.
complexity.summary: Copies and sorts the array, then runs a two-pointer scan to find the pair summing to target, and finally recovers original 1-indexed positions via linear index() searches (with a special case when both values coincide at the same first index).

complexity.notes: The validity check is O(k^2) per line (line.count inside a loop over k elements), which is fine for fixed k=9 but would scale poorly if generalized; a set-based check would be O(k). Using 'valid *= isValidLine(...)' with booleans is terse but unconventional; 'valid = valid and isValidLine(...)' or all() would be more idiomatic. Note the solution checks every line fully rather than short-circuiting on the first invalid line (list.count and the loop over all lines always run), so even the average case does constant work.
complexity.summary: Extracts all 9 rows, 9 columns (via list comprehension), and 9 sub-boxes (via slicing arithmetic), then validates each line by scanning it and using list.count to detect duplicate digits. Since the board is always a fixed 9x9 grid, all work is constant time and constant space.

complexity.notes: Correct but slightly clunky: the elif chain pops the stack during condition evaluation via short-circuiting, which works here but is easy to misread; a constant dict mapping closers to openers (e.g. {')':'(', '}':'{', ']':'['}) plus a single pop/compare would be cleaner. Also, membership testing against the list ['(', '{', '['] is fine (fixed size 3), but a set literal or string would be more idiomatic.
complexity.summary: Classic stack-based validation: push each opening bracket, and on each closing bracket pop and verify it matches the corresponding opener; the string is valid iff the stack ends empty with no mismatch or early pop on an empty stack.

complexity.notes: The dict keys come from a fixed 3-element literal, so collisions are bounded and lookups are O(1) even in the worst case. Checking membership with `bracket in "({["` is fine here given the tiny alphabet; a set literal would be marginally more idiomatic but no faster asymptotically.
complexity.summary: Classic stack-based validation: push opening brackets, and on each closing bracket check that it matches the most recent unmatched opener via a fixed closing-to-opening map. Returns true only if the stack is empty at the end.
